Adjustments to the survey process should be made as necessary, including changes to the counting area, recruitment techniques, team operations, or other procedures to optimize performance. 2. Leverage the strengths of survey team members by identifying the most effective recruiters based on the quality of their recruitment efforts. Determine which team members perform best at specific venues and with particular populations. 3. Foster team morale by recognizing excellent work and encouraging mutual support and collaboration among team members. 4. A sampling event concludes either at the end of the designated venue-day-time period or when the maximum number of participants has been enrolled. 5. At the end of each sampling event, a post-event debriefing should be conducted to allow field staff to discuss any issues or special circumstances encountered. This debriefing can take the form of a group meeting with all field staff or one-on-one conversations. 6. Potential discussion questions during the debriefing include: How did the sampling event go overall? Were there any site-related issues that impacted project activities? Were there any barriers to recruitment, and what strategies proved successful? Were there any challenges with HIV test specimen collection or test kits? Were there difficulties with HIV testing and counseling? 7. If necessary, the field supervisor should document this information in the appropriate forms and notify the principal investigator or other staff if amendments to the standard operating procedures (SOP) or protocol are required. 8. The field supervisor should record notes about the sampling event, documenting any barriers to survey activities, changes at the venue, or safety issues. This information is critical for interpreting recruitment statistics and improving operations. 9. The field supervisor should collect all materials used during the sampling event, review them for accuracy, make corrections as needed, and tabulate recruitment outcomes. 10. Express gratitude to any gatekeepers or individuals who facilitated the sampling process at the venue. 11. Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) surveys involve a complex, multi-step process for participant recruitment, enrollment, and participation. These steps include data collection, survey implementation, quality assurance, and data analysis. 12. Participation in an RDS survey typically requires two visits to the survey site. The first visit includes coupon verification, eligibility screening, informed consent, interview administration, biological specimen collection and testing, recruitment training, and compensation for time and transportation. 13. The second visit involves returning any remaining test results, conducting a recruitment effort interview, and providing compensation for successful peer referrals. 14. Upon arrival at the survey site, potential participants are greeted by a receptionist who verifies their coupon validity and ensures they meet eligibility criteria. 15. Eligibility screening often involves sensitive questions and should be conducted in a private area. The screener must determine whether the individual is a member of the target population. 16. Informed consent must be obtained before conducting any survey procedures. This involves reviewing the consent form with the participant, answering any questions, and obtaining either written or verbal consent, depending on the protocol. 17. After informed consent is obtained, the participant is enrolled in the survey, and the interview process begins. 18. Participants should receive pre-test counseling before providing biological specimens. Consent for the interview and specimen collection may be obtained together or separately. 19. Participants may decline to provide biological specimens for various reasons, such as fear or unfamiliarity with the process. Any changes in consent should be documented and respected. 20. After the interview and specimen collection, participants are given coupons to recruit peers into the survey. Each coupon has a unique code linked to the participant’s own coupon. 21. Survey staff should train participants on how to recruit peers, emphasizing the importance of safeguarding coupons, recruiting only eligible individuals, and explaining the survey’s purpose and procedures. 22. Compensation for participation should be provided only to those who complete at least the interview. Participants should also receive risk-reduction materials such as condoms, lubricants, syringes, and educational materials on HIV and other STIs. 23. Issues with compensation may arise if participants inquire about which of their recruits have participated. Providing such information could compromise confidentiality and is not recommended. 24. Test results should be returned to participants as needed, and those with positive STI test results should be referred for treatment or care.
